content: Interstitial fluid, also known as tissue fluid or intercellular fluid, is a solution that surrounds and bathes the cells of multicellular animals. It constitutes the primary component of extracellular fluid, which also includes plasma and transcellular fluid. Approximately 4 imperial gallons of interstitial fluid are present in the human body, serving to supply nutrients to cells and facilitate the removal of waste products. Plasma and interstitial fluid share a similar composition. Plasma, the major component of blood, freely exchanges with interstitial fluid through pores and intercellular clefts in the capillary endothelium. The formation of tissue fluid is driven by hydrostatic pressure, which is generated by the pumping action of the heart. This pressure forces water out of the capillaries. Large solutes, unable to pass through the capillary walls, create a water potential gradient that induces osmosis. Water moves from areas of higher concentration to lower concentration in an attempt to achieve equilibrium, drawing water back into the vessels. However, due to the continuous flow of blood in the capillaries, equilibrium is never fully reached. The balance between hydrostatic and osmotic pressures varies along the length of the capillaries. At the arterial end, hydrostatic pressure exceeds osmotic pressure, resulting in a net movement of water and solutes into the tissue fluid. Conversely, at the venous end, osmotic pressure predominates, favoring the reabsorption of substances back into the capillaries. This dynamic is influenced by the direction of blood flow and the solute imbalances created by the net movement of water into the tissue fluid. The removal of tissue fluid is facilitated by the lymphatic system, which prevents its accumulation around cells. Tissue fluid enters surrounding lymphatic vessels and eventually rejoins the bloodstream. When the removal process is impaired, tissue fluid can accumulate, leading to swelling, a condition often observed in the feet and ankles due to the effects of gravity. An example of such swelling is elephantiasis. Interstitial fluid is composed of a water-based solvent containing amino acids, sugars, fatty acids, coenzymes, hormones, neurotransmitters, salts, and cellular waste products. Its composition varies depending on the exchanges between the cells and the blood in different tissues and regions of the body. Not all blood components pass into the tissue fluid; for instance, red blood cells, platelets, and plasma proteins are too large to traverse the capillary walls. As a result, tissue fluid is essentially blood plasma without the plasma proteins. It also contains certain types of white blood cells that help combat infections. Lymph, a component of interstitial fluid, is returned to the circulatory system by the lymphatic system, which also recycles proteins and excess interstitial fluid. Physiologically, interstitial fluid plays a critical role in bathing the cells of tissues. It facilitates the delivery of nutrients and other materials to cells, supports intercellular communication, and aids in the removal of metabolic waste products.
